name: AVL Tree
description: A self-balancing Binary Search Tree where the heights of two child subtrees of any node differ by at most one. Named after inventors Adelson-Velsky and Landis (1962).
aim: Maintain a height-balanced BST so that insert, delete, and search always run in O(log n) worst case — unlike unbalanced BSTs which degrade to O(n).
howItWorks: Insert using standard BST insert rules
After each insert, update balance factors (BF = left height − right height) going back up the path
If any node has |BF| > 1, the tree is unbalanced — perform the appropriate rotation
LL Case (BF > 1, new node in left-left): Single Right Rotation
RR Case (BF < -1, new node in right-right): Single Left Rotation
LR Case (BF > 1, new node in left-right): Left Rotation on child, then Right Rotation on node
RL Case (BF < -1, new node in right-left): Right Rotation on child, then Left Rotation on node
After rotation, update heights — tree is balanced again

time.averageCase: Tree stays balanced — height is always O(log n)
time.worstCase: Guaranteed even for sorted input — rotations prevent O(n) degradation

complexity.spaceDescription: O(n) for storing n nodes; O(log n) call stack during insert/search

realWorld: Linux kernel: uses AVL-like red-black trees for scheduling and memory management
Database indexes: many database engines use balanced BST variants for O(log n) range queries
C++ STL std::map and std::set use red-black trees (AVL variant) internally
Java TreeMap and TreeSet use red-black trees derived from AVL concepts
whenToUse: When you need guaranteed O(log n) search, insert, and delete
When data arrives in sorted order (unbalanced BST would degrade to O(n))
When read-heavy workloads justify the rotation overhead on insert
alternatives: Red-Black Tree: fewer rotations on insert, slightly less balanced height — preferred in practice (used by Java, C++ STL)
B-Tree: for disk-based storage where minimizing disk I/O is critical (used in databases)
Skip List: simpler to implement, probabilistically O(log n)

beginnerAnalogy: Think of an AVL tree like a self-adjusting bookshelf that automatically reorganizes when it gets lopsided. If too many books pile up on the left side, it rotates to rebalance — so you can always find any book in the same fast time, no matter how many books are added.
beginnerWhat: A special sorted tree that stays perfectly balanced by automatically rotating parts of itself whenever it gets too uneven.
beginnerWhy: Without balancing, a BST can become a linked list (worst case O(n) search). AVL rotations guarantee O(log n) always.
beginnerWhen: When you need fast, guaranteed lookup times even when inserting data in sorted order.
